name: Liam Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Liam, thanks for taking the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say is confidential and won't carry your name. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. As long as I'm not on the news.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You won't be. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter for a big contractor putting up two apartment towers down by the old docks, twenty-two floors each. My crew does first fix, so the stud walls, door frames and window boards before the plasterers come. Dave, the foreman, says I measure with my eyes shut, because I'm still slow and I've had to redo a whole corridor of door frames once. I like the view from the top floors and the fact that it's steady work, years of it. What wears me out is the hoist queue in the morning, you can stand there twenty minutes with your tools waiting to go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. Less noise, more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop hearing about it. Sean and I would have a laugh about the guy at the toolbox talk who said robots would be fitting door frames by now. I'd maybe put something on social media, but I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan carries on. I want to run my own small firm one day, like my uncle Tomasz does, doing kitchens and extensions. I've got a flat I bought with my savings and a bit of help from my grandparents, and I rent it out, so I'm in a decent spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the towers, get faster, get my full qualification next year. I'd start putting money aside for a van and a proper set of tools, so in three or four years I can go out on my own. I'd keep doing the odd weekend job my uncle passes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your uncle's firm. What makes you want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got two vans and three lads, and nobody tells him what to do. He started at my age with a borrowed drill. My dad always says Tomasz worked for it, nobody handed it to him, and that's how I want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. When Tomasz passes me a weekend job, I use one of those apps to help write the quote so it looks professional. Sean showed me. I don't use it for the actual work, that's still in my head and on my tape.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can stop hearing about it. Sean and I would laugh about the toolbox talk where someone said robots would be fitting door frames by now.
S0.think: My plan carries on: run my own small firm one day like my uncle Tomasz. I've got a flat I bought and rent out, so I'm in a decent spot.
S0.do: Keeps working on the towers, aiming to get faster and qualify next year. Starts putting money aside for a van and a proper set of tools to go out on his own in three or four years, while doing weekend jobs from his uncle.
S0.quote: He started at my age with a borrowed drill.
S0.fieldNote: Liam's cushion is partly a rental flat bought with savings and help from his grandparents. His plan to run his own firm is modelled on his uncle and framed as earning it, not being handed it. He uses AI in a limited way for paperwork, copied from a friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that one seems likely. Some things change, but somebody's still got to build stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who work hard and learn will be fine, like always. Businesses adapt, that's what they do. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let firms sort it, but maybe fund apprenticeships properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly fine for me. On our towers there's already talk of factory-made bathroom pods that just get craned in, and I can see more of that coming. But someone still has to fit them, and when I've got my own firm, I'm doing kitchens in people's houses, not towers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the towers and my qualification, and once a few of the lads are using a new tool and it actually works, I'd learn it. I'd use the AI apps more for quotes and pricing, maybe for ordering, the way Tomasz has started doing. And I'd keep saving for the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should keep out of the way. Even if lots of people need to change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yeah. I'd rather see money go into apprenticeships, where people learn a real skill from someone who knows it, than just paying people to sit at home. My grandad came here with nothing and worked. That's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomasz? How does he handle new things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's slow to start but then he goes all in. He held out on a laser level for years, and now he's got three. I'm probably the same.

S1.say: I'd say people who work hard and learn will be fine, like always, and businesses adapt. The government should keep out of the way but fund apprenticeships properly.
S1.think: It's mostly fine for me: factory-made bathroom pods will spread on towers, but someone still fits them. Once I've got my own firm I'll be doing kitchens in people's houses, not towers.
S1.do: Keeps on with the towers and his qualification, learning new tools once colleagues have proved them. Uses AI apps more for quotes, pricing and ordering, and keeps saving for the van.
S1.quote: He held out on a laser level for years, and now he's got three.
S1.fieldNote: His free-market view is tempered by support for apprenticeships, which he sees as earning rather than handouts. He follows the pattern of his uncle: slow to start, then fully in. He sees his future in house work rather than big sites, which he thinks is safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That would kill the firm before it existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stick together, families especially, and not wait for the government to save them. I'd say small businesses need protecting from the big tech companies. I'd probably share a few posts about it, which I don't normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my plan's dead. Nobody's going to hire a new one-man kitchen firm if a robot crew can do it cheaper next year. The flat's the only thing that keeps me steady, because rent keeps coming in, at least for a while, if my tenant still has a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the van, no point. I'd cut back hard, no holidays, no new car, and put more money into the savings. I'd keep the flat and its rent coming in, and if it came to it, I'd move back to my parents' and let Kasia stay at hers for a bit, or we'd both go to mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I had something to hold on to, because of the flat, but the plan I had would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your tenant might not have a job either. Who is your tenant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young woman who works in a bank call centre. Lovely, always pays on time. Thinking about it, her job would probably go before mine. So the flat's only safe if somebody somewhere still has money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move back to your parents'. How would that feel at twenty-nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit embarrassing. But my dad would just say that's what family's for. In our house, nobody would think twice about it.

S2.say: I'd say people need to stick together, families especially, and not wait for the government to save them. Small businesses need protecting from the big tech companies.
S2.think: My plan's dead, because nobody will hire a new one-man kitchen firm if a robot crew is cheaper. The rented flat is the only thing that keeps me steady, if my tenant still has a job.
S2.do: Stops saving for the van and cuts back hard on holidays and a new car, putting more into savings. Keeps the rented flat for its income and would move back in with his parents if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious but still holding on to something, though his plan would be gone.
S2.quote: So the flat's only safe if somebody somewhere still has money.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture destroys his business dream more than his immediate income. He works out live that his rental income depends on his tenant's job, which is itself exposed. Family support is his natural fallback, and he'd accept it without much shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd get to start the firm, and then watch it go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make some money and get ready, so don't sit about. I'd say people should start their own things now, while there's time. And I'd say government should cut red tape so small firms can move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd wonder whether it's worth starting at all. Buy a van, build up customers for three years, and then the robots come. But maybe three good years is still worth more than three years on the towers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see how quickly the robots actually show up on sites. If it looks real, I'd start doing more weekend jobs with Tomasz instead of buying my own van, so I'm earning without a big outlay. And I'd keep saving harder, because whatever happens, I'd want a bigger pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd think about it on the drive in most mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why work with Tomasz rather than start your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's already got the vans and the customers. If it all ends in five years, I'd rather not be stuck with a loan on a van nobody needs. It's not what I wanted, but it's the sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses adapt. Would Tomasz adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd try. He'd probably buy whatever robot comes first and work out how to use it. Whether a small firm with one robot beats a big firm with a hundred, I honestly don't know.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to make money and get ready, so don't sit about, and people should start their own things now. Government should cut red tape so small firms can move fast.
S3.think: I'd wonder whether it's worth starting a firm at all if the robots come in three years. But three good years might still beat three years on the towers.
S3.do: Waits a year to see how fast robots reach sites. If it looks real, takes on more weekend jobs with his uncle instead of buying his own van, and saves harder to build a bigger cushion.
S3.feel: Anxious, thinking about it on most morning drives.
S3.quote: I'd rather not be stuck with a loan on a van nobody needs.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline forces a real trade-off between his dream and caution, and he chooses caution. Working through his uncle's firm is a compromise he admits isn't what he wanted. He's honest that he doesn't know whether small firms can compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a proper go at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Get a trade, build something, be ready. I'd say we don't need the government planning everyone's lives, just keep taxes down and let people get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think this is my chance. Ten years is long enough to start a firm, build it up and maybe even be the one buying robots instead of being replaced by them. Like Tomasz with his laser levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead and buy the van and tools in about three years, like I planned, and start my firm. I'd use AI properly for the business side, quotes, invoices, ordering, from day one. And when robots for kitchens and extensions get good and the price comes down, I'd buy one and use it in the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. But mostly fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot for your own firm. Would you still hire lads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, at first, I'd want a couple of young ones learning like I did. Later on, I don't know. If the robot does the job and the customer wants it cheaper, I'd have to think about it. I wouldn't like letting anyone go, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kasia that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've got ten years to build something, and I want to do it. She'd probably say she's heard me say that for three years already. She'd be right, but this time I'd have a reason to hurry.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work: get a trade, build something, be ready. We don't need government planning everyone's lives, just low taxes.
S4.think: This is my chance to start a firm, build it up and be the one buying robots instead of being replaced by them. Like Tomasz with his laser levels.
S4.do: Buys the van and tools in about three years as planned and starts his own firm. Uses AI for quotes, invoices and ordering from day one, and buys a kitchen-fitting robot for the firm once prices come down.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly fired up.
S4.quote: She'd probably say she's heard me say that for three years already.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, the threat becomes his opportunity to own the machines as a business owner. He's uncomfortable about eventually replacing his own workers but doesn't rule it out. His girlfriend's teasing shows he's talked about the firm for years without starting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It kills the firm before I've started and I'd be leaning on my parents at twenty-nine. What would help is proper apprenticeships for whatever's still needed, and cheap loans or tax breaks so small firms can buy the same machines as the big ones. Not people being paid to sit at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me will actually move. I talk about the firm a lot. I've been about to start it for three years. Ten years of warning might just be ten years of being about to start.

headlineQuote: Ten years of warning might just be ten years of being about to start.
portrait: Liam Kowalski is a 27-year-old junior carpenter doing first fix on two apartment towers, who owns a rented-out flat and dreams of running his own firm like his uncle Tomasz. He believes in hard work, family and apprenticeships over handouts, and uses AI now and then for quotes. He's calm about the milder pictures, anxious in the fast AGI picture because his business plan dies and his rental income depends on his tenant's job. Five years pushes him into a cautious compromise with his uncle, while ten years makes him want to start his firm and buy robots himself. He admits he's been about to start for three years already.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it kills his plan for a firm before he starts and he'd be leaning on his parents at twenty-nine.
whatWouldHelp: Proper apprenticeships for remaining work, and cheap loans or tax breaks so small firms can buy the same machines as big ones.
